Order in Partial Markov Categories Volume: NN Journal: Electronic Notes in Theoretical Informatics and Computer Science Volume: NN
Elena Di Lavore a, Mario Román a, Paweł Sobociński b, Márk Széles c

Abstract
Partial Markov categories are a recent framework for categorical probability theory, providing an abstract account of partial probabilistic computation. In this article, we discuss two order relations on the morphisms of a partial Markov category. In particular, we prove that every partial Markov category is canonically enriched over the category of preordered sets and monotone maps. We show that our construction recovers several well-known order enrichments. We also demonstrate that the existence of codiagonal maps (comparators) is closely related to order properties of partial Markov categories. We propose a synthetic version of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to facilitate inequational reasoning in partial Markov categories. We apply this new axiom to prove that updating a prior distribution with an evidence predicate increases the likelihood of the evidence in the posterior.



keywords

Markov categories, preorder enrichment, string diagrams,
probabilistic inference, copy-discard categories

1
Introduction

Markov categories
[
Fri20
,
CJ19
]
are a
synthetic framework for probability theory. They allow us to reason
about probabilistic processes using a few basic axioms that model key
aspects of probabilistic computation. Morphisms in a Markov category
can be composed both in sequence and in parallel, via a symmetric
monoidal structure. Every object is equipped with a
commutative comonoid, which allows for copying and discarding
information. An important axiom is the existence of
conditionals
,
which are an abstraction of conditional probability distributions.
This simple setting has been successfully applied to various areas in
probability theory
[
CFG+24
,
FK23
,
Jac21
]
, semantics
of probabilistic programming

[
Ste21
,
SS21
,
AFK+24
]
,
causal inference

[
JKZ21
,
LT23
,
YZ22
]

and information theory
[
Per24
]
.

Morphisms in Markov categories can be thought of as total probabilistic
computations. Totality is encoded by an axiom – naturality of
discarding – declaring that
maps can be discarded without affecting the meaning of the process.
However, many operations in probability theory are inherently
partial. An important example is bayesian updating: if one tries to
learn from evidence that is
incompatible with the prior belief, updating is impossible. Markov
categories lack the structure to express this partiality.

In order to express partiality, we need to drop naturality of discarding, and
thus work with copy-discard (CD) categories

[
CJ19
,
CG99
]
.
Morphisms in such copy-discard categories correspond to partial probabilistic
computations. We would like to highlight two recent works following
this approach. In
[
LT23
]
, the authors start from a
copy-discard category, and derive
conditional distributions from equality comparison and
normalisation
of
subprobability kernels. While the theory is elegant, it is mostly suited for
discrete probability. In contrast, the framework of
partial Markov categories

[
DR23
]
starts from a copy-discard category with conditionals. The
advantage of this approach is the abundance of models. Examples of partial
Markov categories include Kleisli-categories of ‘subprobability monads’,
cartesian restriction categories

[
CL02
,
CL03
,
CL07
]
, and
cartesian bicategories of relations
[
CW87
]
.

The main contribution of this paper is to show that every
partial Markov
category
is enriched (in the sense of
[
Kel82
]
) in the
category of partial orders and monotone
maps. That is, every hom-set in a
partial Markov category
is a
preorder, and the operations
of the symmetric monoidal category structure are monotone with
respect to this preorder.
The existence of such an order-enrichment makes the setting
particularly appealing for developing the basics of inequational
reasoning in synthetic probability theory. This is important, since
some crucial properties of bayesian reasoning are inequational, such
as the fact that updating a prior with evidence
increases the likelihood of the evidence being true in the posterior.

This paper is structured as follows. In Section
2
we
recall the basic theory of
partial Markov categories
. We also
introduce some running examples. In Section

3
, we define the preorder enrichment on partial
Markov categories; we display several well-known order enrichments as instances
of our construction. Section
4
is dedicated to the
study of least conditionals in
partial Markov categories
. Our main results in
this section are about the relationship of least conditionals and the existence
of comparators (Theorems
4.6
and

4.9
). Finally, Section
5

is an application of the conditional preorder. We derive a synthetic analogue of
the validity-increase theorem, under suitable assumptions (Theorem

5.16
).

Throughout this paper we will use string-diagrammatic notation
with the diagrams written from left to right. For a detailed
introduction to string-diagrammatic calculi, see

[
Sel10
]
. Occasionally, we will also apply
equational reasoning. To ease notation, we will treat all monoidal
categories as if they were strict.

Related work

Inequalities play an important role in the theory of cartesian restriction categories
[
CL02
]
and cartesian bicategories of relations
[
CW87
]
.
In fact, restriction categories have a canonical ordering on
morphisms
[
CL02
, §2.1.4]
and can be seen as
enriched categories
[
CG14
]
. Similarly, morphisms in
bicategories of relations have a canonical ordering that forms an
enrichment
[
Nes24
]
.
These canonical inequalities are instances of the ordering we
introduce
in this paper, see Propositions
3.19

and
3.21
.

Order enrichments for categories of probabilistic maps have been
considered before, in the context of effectus
theory
[
CJWW15
,
Cho19
,
Jac18
]
.
One of the anonymous reviewers pointed out that the recently introduced quasi-Markov categories

[
FGL+25
]
are poset-enriched by the restriction order; comparing in detail the order in

partial Markov categories
and quasi-Markov categories, both generalisations of

cartesian restriction categories
, is left for future work.

2
Preliminaries

Copy-discard categories
(Definition
2.9
) are theories of
processes – symmetric monoidal categories – where resources can be copied and
discarded.
Partial Markov categories
are
copy-discard categories
that
additionally have
conditionals
: a factorization property often needed in
categorical probability.

We go a step further and explicitly introduce
copy-discard-compare (CDC)
categories
(Definition
2.9
): theories of
processes where we can assert the equality of two resources (“compare” them).

Discrete partial Markov categories
are copy-discard-compare categories with

conditionals
(Definition

2.10
). Table

1
summarises the terminology related to
variations of
copy-discard categories
.

Structure

Maps are

Comparators/caps

Conditionals

✓

Cartesian restriction category

deterministic

deterministic

✓

[
FGL+25
]

Table 1
:
Types of copy-discard categories. In each row, the
structure entails all properties
listed or marked with (✓).

Definition 2.1
.

(Copy-discard category)

A
copy-discard category

[
CG99
,
CJ19
]
is a symmetric
monoidal
category
(\mathsf{C},\otimes,I)
in which every object
X
has a
compatible commutative
comonoid
structure, consisting of a counit or
discard
,
\varepsilon_{X}\colon X\to I
; and a
comultiplication or
copy
,
\delta_{X}\colon X\to X\otimes X
, satisfying the following
axioms.

1
.

(1)

Comultiplication is associative,
\delta_{X}\fatsemi(\delta_{X}\otimes\mathrm{id}{})=\delta_{X}\fatsemi(\mathrm{id}{}\otimes\delta_{X}).

(2)

Counit is neutral for comultiplication,
\delta_{X}\fatsemi(\varepsilon_{X}\otimes\mathrm{id}{})=\mathrm{id}{}=\delta_{X}\fatsemi(\mathrm{id}{}\otimes\varepsilon_{X}).

(3)

Comultiplication is commutative,
\delta_{X}\fatsemi\sigma_{X,X}=\delta_{X}
,
where
\sigma_{X,X}:X\otimes X\to X\otimes X
is the symmetry.

(4)

Comultiplication is uniform,
\delta_{X\otimes Y}=(\delta_{X}\otimes\delta_{Y})\fatsemi(\mathrm{id}{}\otimes\sigma\otimes\mathrm{id}{})
, and
\delta_{I}=\mathrm{id}{}
.

(5)

Counit is uniform,
\varepsilon_{X\otimes Y}=\varepsilon_{X}\otimes\varepsilon_{Y}
and
\varepsilon_{I}=\mathrm{id}{}
.

Notably, counits and comultiplications are not required to form natural
transformations.

Figure 1
:
Structure and axioms of a commutative comonoid.

The language of
copy-discard categories
can express when
morphisms are ‘deterministic’, ‘total’ and ‘total on their domain of
definition’ (quasi-total).

Definition 2.2
.

(Deterministic, total)
A morphism
f\colon X\to Y
in a
copy-discard category
is
deterministic if it commutes with the copy,
f\mathbin{\fatsemi}\delta_{Y}=\delta_{X}\mathbin{\fatsemi}(f\otimes f)
. It is total if it commutes with the
discard,
f\mathbin{\fatsemi}\varepsilon_{Y}=\varepsilon_{X}
.

Definition 2.3
.

(Restriction
[
DR23
,
LT23
]
)
Let
\mathsf{C}
be a
copy-discard category
.

(1)

We say that a map
f:X\to Y
is a
restriction
of

g:X\to Y
if
f=\delta_{X}\mathbin{\fatsemi}(g\otimes(f\mathbin{\fatsemi}\varepsilon_{Y}))
. In this
situation, we write
f\preceq g
. See Figure
2

for an illustration.

(2)

A map
f
is called
quasi-total
if
f\preceq f
. Clearly, all deterministic and total maps are
quasi-total.

The collection of quasi-total maps is partially ordered by
restriction
[
LT23
, Lemma 98]
.

Figure 2
:
The normalisation order

Definition 2.4
.

The
conditional composition
of two morphisms,
f\colon X\to A
and

g\colon A\otimes X\to B
, of a
copy-discard category
, is the morphism defined by the equation in Figure
3
.
In other words,
conditional composition
passes a copy of the input and the
output of the first morphism to the second morphism.

Figure 3
:
Conditional composition.

Definition 2.5
.

(Conditionals)

A
copy-discard category
has
conditionals
if
every morphism
f\colon X\to A\otimes B
can be decomposed as

f=(f\mathbin{\fatsemi}(\mathrm{id}_{A}\otimes\varepsilon_{B}))\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}c
, for
some quasi-total
c\colon A\otimes X\to B
. In this
situation we say that
x
is a conditional of
f
.
For morphisms
f\colon X\to A
and
g\colon A\to B
, a

bayesian inverse
of
g
with respect to
f
is a
conditional
g^{\hyperlink{linkbayesinv}{\dagger}}_{f}\colon B\otimes X\to A
of
f\mathbin{\fatsemi}\delta_{A}\mathbin{\fatsemi}(g\otimes\mathrm{id})
.

Requiring
conditionals
to be quasi-total is natural but not
strictly necessary for some of our developments. However, assuming
quasi-totality is crucial to guarantee that

conditionals
of a morphism are partially ordered. The
proof of Theorem
4.9
also relies on

conditionals
being quasi-total.

Definition 2.6
.

(Partial Markov category
[
DR23
]
)

A
partial Markov category
is a
copy-discard category
with

conditionals
.

Remark 2.7
.

In a partial Markov category,
f\preceq f
if and only if
f\mathbin{\fatsemi}\varepsilon
is deterministic
[
DR23
, Proposition 3.5]
.

We will later work with a particular subclass of
copy-discard categories
:
those that are
balanced
.
Balanced

copy-discard categories

cover a large class of examples, and they are particularly well-behaved with
respect to the partial order we introduce in
Definition
3.1
. The name

balanced
is related to properties of idempotent
morphisms, see
[
FGL+23
, Theorem 4.1.8.]
.

Definition 2.8
.

(Balanced copy-discard category
[
FGL+23
]
)
A
copy-discard category

\mathsf{C}
is
balanced
if the
following implication holds for all appropriately typed morphisms.

Being
balanced
was introduced as the
Cauchy–Schwarz
property

[
FGL+23
, Definition A.5.1]
; we avoid this name to avoid
confusion with the synthetic version of the
Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
we
introduce later. However, we recall that there are at least two other
unrelated notions of
balanced category
in the literature

[
Sel10
,
Joh14
]
. This should cause to confusion
in the current context.

Definition 2.9
.

(Copy-Discard-Compare category)

A
copy-discard-compare category
is a
copy-discard category
in
which every object,
X
, has a compatible partial Frobenius structure,
consisting of an additional commutative multiplication, or

comparator
,
\mu_{X}\colon X\otimes X\to X
,
satisfying the following axioms.

(1)

Multiplication is associative,
(\mu_{X}\otimes\mathrm{id}{})\fatsemi\mu_{X}=(\mathrm{id}{}\otimes\mu_{X})\fatsemi\mu_{X}
.

(2)

Multiplication is commutative,
\sigma_{X,X}\fatsemi\mu_{X}=\mu_{X}
.

(3)

Multiplication is right inverse to comultiplication,
\delta_{X}\fatsemi\mu_{X}=\mathrm{id}{}
.

(4)

Multiplication satisfies the Frobenius rule,
(\delta_{X}\otimes\mathrm{id}{})\fatsemi(\mathrm{id}{}\otimes\mu_{X})=\mu_{X}\fatsemi\delta_{X}=(\mathrm{id}{}\otimes\delta_{X})\fatsemi(\mu_{X}\otimes\mathrm{id}{}).

(5)

Multiplication is uniform,
\mu_{X\otimes Y}=(\mathrm{id}{}\otimes\sigma_{Y,X}\otimes\mathrm{id}{})\fatsemi(\mu_{X}\otimes\mu_{Y})
, and
\mu_{I}=\mathrm{id}{}
.

Figure 4
:
Structure and axioms of comparators.

Definition 2.10
.

(Discrete Partial Markov category
[
DR23
]
)

A
discrete partial Markov category
is a
copy-discard-compare
category
with
conditionals
.

We provide an alternative characterization of
copy-discard-compare
categories
via
cap
morphisms. This is the approach followed by
Lorenz and Tull
[
LT23
]
, where it was mentioned that the
presentations via
caps
and comparators are equivalent. We
provide a proof for completeness.

Definition 2.11
.

(Caps
[
LT23
, Definition 6]
)

A
copy-discard category
is said to have
caps
if it is
equipped with a family of
morphisms
\cap_{X}:X\otimes X\to I
, satisfying the following axioms.

(1)

Caps are commutative,

\sigma_{X,X}\fatsemi\cap_{X}=\cap_{X}
.

(2)

Caps interact with the comultiplication,

\delta_{X}\mathbin{\fatsemi}\cap_{X}=\varepsilon_{X}
.

(3)

Caps satisfy the Frobenius rule,
(\delta_{X}\otimes\mathrm{id}{})\fatsemi(\mathrm{id}{}\otimes\cap_{X})=(\mathrm{id}{}\otimes\delta_{X})\fatsemi(\cap_{X}\otimes\mathrm{id}{})
.

(4)

Caps are uniform,
\cap_{X\otimes Y}=(\mathrm{id}{}\otimes\sigma_{Y,X}\otimes\mathrm{id}{})\fatsemi(\cap_{X}\otimes\cap_{Y})
, and
\cap_{I}=\mathrm{id}{}
.

Figure 5
:
Structure and axioms of caps.

Proposition 2.12
.

A
copy-discard category
is a
copy-discard-compare category
if and
only if it has
caps
.

Proof 2.13
.

Assume that
\mathsf{C}
is a
copy-discard-compare category
. We may define

caps
via
\cap_{X}=\mu_{X}\fatsemi\varepsilon_{X}
; the
cap
axioms
follow immediately.

Conversely, assume that
\mathsf{C}
has
caps
. Define the comparator as one
of the two sides of the Frobenius rule (
3
),

\mu_{X}=(\delta_{X}\otimes\mathrm{id}{})\fatsemi(\mathrm{id}{}\otimes\cap_{X})=(\mathrm{id}{}\otimes\delta_{X})\fatsemi(\cap_{X}\otimes\mathrm{id}{})
.

First, we show commutativity using (
a
) the definition of the compare
map, (
b
) naturality of symmetries, (
c
) commutativity of the

cap
, and (
d
) commutativity of copy.

For associativity, we use (
a
) the definition of the compare map, and
(
b
) associativity of copy.

The rest of this section introduces some
partial Markov categories
that we will use as
running examples.

2.1
Example: subprobability kernels

The category
\mathsf{BorelStoch}_{\leq 1}
of standard Borel spaces and measurable
subprobability kernels is a
discrete partial Markov
category

[
DR23
]
. The subcategory
\mathsf{FinStoch}_{\leq 1}\hookrightarrow\mathsf{BorelStoch}_{\leq 1}
of finite sets and substochastic matrices is
also a
discrete partial Markov category
. One can see that both
\mathsf{BorelStoch}_{\leq 1}

and
\mathsf{FinStoch}_{\leq 1}
are
balanced
, by essentially the same argument as in

[
FGL+23
, Proposition A.5.2.]
.

2.2
Example: cartesian restriction categories

cartesian restriction
categories

[
CL02
,
CL03
,
CL07
]

are an abstraction of the category
\mathsf{Par}
of sets and partial functions. They
are
copy-discard categories
where comultiplication is natural, i.e. all
morphisms are deterministic but not necessarily total.

Discrete cartesian restriction categories
are cartesian
restriction
categories with a comparator.
We now show that
cartesian restriction categories
have
conditionals
.
That is,
cartesian restriction categories
are
partial Markov
categories
where all morphisms are deterministic.

Proposition 2.14
.

All
cartesian restriction categories
are
balanced

partial Markov categories
.

Proof 2.15
.

Morphisms in
cartesian restriction categories
are always deterministic. We
use this fact to show that there are
conditionals
.

Again, because every morphism is deterministic, these

conditionals
are quasi-total, and the category is

balanced
.

2.3
Example: cartesian bicategories of relations

cartesian bicategories of relations
are an abstraction of the
category

\mathsf{Rel}
of sets and relations. They are
copy-discard-compare categories

with extra structure and axioms that give them the expressive power of regular
logic (see Figure
6
). They are also an example
class of
partial Markov categories
.

Proposition 2.16
.

All
cartesian bicategories of relations
are
partial Markov
categories
.

Proof 2.17
.

The compact closed structure and idempotency of convolution give
quasi-total
conditionals
.
We use the syntax of
cartesian bicategories of
relations

[
CW87
]
.
Every morphism in a cartesian bicategory of relations is
quasi-total:
m\preceq m
if and only if
m\mathbin{\fatsemi}\varepsilon
is deterministic (Remark
2.7
),
and this is true because convolution is idempotent (last equation
in Figure
6
applied to
m\mathbin{\fatsemi}\varepsilon
).

[

to get a counterexample in
\mathsf{Rel}
.

3
Conditional inequality

Let us endow
partial Markov categories
with a
preorder-enrichment. We prove
that the
conditional inequality

(Definition
3.1
) is an enrichment
(Theorem
3.4
) and derive basic inequalities.

Definition 3.1
.

(Conditional inequality).
In any
copy-discard category
,
conditional inequality
relates
two parallel morphisms,
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g
for
f\colon X\to Y
and
g\colon X\to Y
, if and only
if there exists some morphism
r\colon Y\otimes X\to I
such that
f=g\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}r
. In this
case, we say that
r

witnesses
the inequality
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g
, and write

f\mathrel{\sqsubseteq^{r}}g
.

Proposition 3.2
.

Conditional inequality

({\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq})
is a preorder.

Proof 3.3
.

Reflexivity is witnessed by the discard morphism,
f\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}\varepsilon=f
, as on
the left below. Let us prove transitivity. If we assume
f\mathrel{\sqsubseteq^{r}}g

and
g\mathrel{\sqsubseteq^{s}}h
, then by associativity of conditional composition,
f=g\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}r=(h\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}s)\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}r=h\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}(s\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}r)
. Thus,
s\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}r
witnesses
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}h
, as on
the right below.

Theorem 3.4
.

Any
partial Markov category
is a preorder-enriched symmetric monoidal category.

Proof 3.5
.

We show that the preorder
({\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq})
on hom-sets is respected by
composition and monoidal products.

Assuming that
g\mathrel{\sqsubseteq^{r}}g^{\prime}
, we can see that
f\fatsemi g{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}f\fatsemi g^{\prime}

by

f\fatsemi g=f\fatsemi(g^{\prime}\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}r)=(f\fatsemi g^{\prime})\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}(g^{\prime\hyperlink{linkbayesinv}{\dagger}}_{f}\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}(r\otimes\varepsilon)).

Assuming that
g\mathrel{\sqsubseteq^{r}}g^{\prime}
, we can see that
g\fatsemi h{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g^{\prime}\fatsemi h
,
by

g\fatsemi h=(g^{\prime}\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}r)\fatsemi h=(g^{\prime}\fatsemi h)\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}(h^{\hyperlink{linkbayesinv}{\dagger}}_{g^{\prime}}\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}(\varepsilon\otimes r)).

Assuming that
g\mathrel{\sqsubseteq^{r}}g^{\prime}
, we can see that
f\otimes g{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}f\otimes g^{\prime}
, by

f\otimes g=f\otimes(g^{\prime}\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}r)=(f\otimes g^{\prime})\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}(\varepsilon\otimes r).

We proceed analogously to show that
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}f^{\prime}
implies
f\otimes g{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}f^{\prime}\otimes g
.
We showed that composition and tensors are monotone. Therefore, the
conditional preorder is an enrichment.

We collect a few elementary properties of the conditional preorder.

Proposition 3.6
.

Let
\mathsf{C}
be a
discrete partial Markov category
.

(1)

For all
f:X\to Y
,
\delta\fatsemi(f\otimes f)\fatsemi\mu{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}f

(2)

Multiplication and comultiplication form an adjoint
pair
\delta\dashv\mu
in the sense of
2-categories
[
Lac10
]
.
That is,
\mathrm{id}{}{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}\delta\mathbin{\fatsemi}\mu
and
\mu\fatsemi\delta{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}\mathrm{id}{}
.

Proof 3.7
.

For point (i), observe that the equality below left follows from the partial
Frobenius axioms.

For point (ii), the first inequality holds by definition,
while the second one can be derived from the partial Frobenius
axioms, as on the right above.

3.1
Subunital enrichments

One may be interested in
partial Markov categories
with
additional logical structure, e.g. certain effectuses with copiers

[
CJWW15
]
. In such categories, effects
X\to I
can
be viewed as (fuzzy) predicates: for example, the discard map,
\varepsilon_{X}:X\to I
, is interpreted as the ‘true’ predicate. When equipping a

partial Markov category
with a preorder enrichment, one would
reasonably expect truth to be the largest predicate.
Call a preorder enrichment
subunital
if
p\leq\varepsilon_{X}
for
all effects
p:X\to I
.

Proposition 3.8
.

In any
partial Markov category
, the conditional preorder is
subunital.

Proof 3.9
.

By counitality of copy.

Moreover, as the next proposition shows, the conditional
preorder is the least subunital preorder enrichment on a
partial
Markov category
. This property will be useful in
(§
3.3
) where we compare
the conditional preorder to the canonical orderings in our running
examples.

Proposition 3.10
.

Let
(\mathsf{C},\leq)
be a preorder-enriched partial Markov category satisfying
p\leq\varepsilon_{X}
for all effects
p\colon X\to I
.

Then, for any two parallel morphisms,
f,g\colon X\to Y
, the following implication holds:

f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g\implies f\leq g.

An immediate consequence of this is that, if
(\leq)
is a
poset-enrichment, then the conditional preorder is also a poset,
i.e. it is antisymmetric.

.

f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g
be witnessed by
r\colon Y\otimes X\to I
. Then,

3.2
Normalisation and the conditional preorder

In this subsection, we relate the conditional
preorder to the restriction order.

The proof of the following statement is immediate from the relevant
definitions.

Lemma 3.12
.

Let
\mathsf{C}
be
copy-discard category
, and let
f,g:X\to Y
be two
quasi-total parallel morphisms. Then,
f\preceq g

implies
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g
.

Proof 3.13
.

The conditional inequality
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g
is witnessed by
f\mathbin{\fatsemi}\varepsilon_{Y}
.

The converse implication does not hold in general, see Example

3.23
. However, under
certain assumptions, we can derive it for quasi-total maps.

Definition 3.14
.

(Sharp witness property)

A
partial Markov category
,
\mathsf{C}
, satisfies the
sharp witness
property
if each inequality,
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g
, between parallel
quasi-total morphisms,
f,g:X\to Y
, is witnessed by a
deterministic effect
r:Y\otimes X\to I
.

Proposition 3.15
.

Let
\mathsf{C}
be a
balanced

copy-discard category
that satisfies the

sharp witness property
. Let
f,g\colon X\to Y
be parallel
quasi-total maps. Then,
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g
if and only if
f\preceq g
.

Proof 3.16
.

By Lemma
3.12
,
f\preceq g

implies
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g
. For the other direction, we use balance and sharp
witnesses. Suppose
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g
with a sharp witness
r
. Since
f
is
quasi-total, we obtain:

3.3
Examples

We finish this section by instantiating the conditional preorder in
our running examples.

Finitary subdistributions

Let
f,g\colon X\to\mathsf{\mathbf{D}}_{\leq 1}(Y)
be two parallel substochastic
channels in
\mathsf{FinStoch}_{\leq 1}
. The inequality
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g

holds exactly when
f

is pointwise dominated by

g
; that is, for all
y\in Y
and
x\in X
, we have
f(y\mid x)\leq g(y\mid x)
.

To see that
\mathsf{FinStoch}_{\leq 1}
satisfies the sharp witness
property, let
f,g:X\to\mathsf{\mathbf{D}}_{\leq 1}(Y)
be quasi-total such that
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g
.
Then for all

x\in X
either
f(y\mid x)=0
for all
y\in Y
, or
f(y\mid x)=g(y\mid x)
for all
y\in Y
. We can then define
r:Y\otimes X\to\mathsf{\mathbf{D}}_{\leq 1}(1)
as

\displaystyle r(\ast\mid y,x)=\begin{cases}0&\text{ if }f(y^{\prime}\mid x)=0\text{ for all }y^{\prime}\in Y\\
1&\text{ otherwise }.\end{cases}

Clearly, this
r
witnesses the inequality
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g
.

Standard Borel spaces and subprobability kernels

One can define a pointwise order on parallel maps
f,g:(X,\sigma_{X})\to(Y,\sigma_{Y})
in
\mathsf{BorelStoch}_{\leq 1}
by setting
f\leq g

if and only if
f(T\mid x)\leq g(T\mid x)
for all points
x\in X
and measurable sets
T\in\sigma_{Y}
. This pointwise order is
a subunital enrichment, see e.g.
[
Cho19
, Proposition 3.2.7. and
Section 3.3.2.]
. The next proposition shows that the
conditional preorder coincides with the pointwise order.

Proposition 3.17
.

For any two parallel morphisms
f,g:(X,\sigma_{X})\to(Y,\sigma_{Y})
in
\mathsf{BorelStoch}_{\leq 1}
,
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g
if and only if

f\leq g
.

Proof 3.18
.

(\Rightarrow)
The first implication is immediate from Proposition

3.10
.

(\Leftarrow)
Let
f\leq g
pointwise. The Radon-Nikodým Theorem for
kernels (see
[
VO18
, Theorem 10]
) states that there
exists
an
r:(Y,\sigma_{Y})\times(X,\sigma_{X})\to[0,\infty]
such that
f(A\mid x)=\int_{A}r(y,x)\cdot g(dy|x)
for all measurable sets
A\in\sigma_{y}
.

It only remains to show that one can pick
r
to be
[0,1]
-valued. Fix an

x\in X
, and let
B_{x}=\{y\in Y\mid r(y,x)>1\}
. This
B_{x}
is clearly
measurable. We show that
g(B_{x}|x)=0
. By assumption,

\int_{B_{x}}r(y,x)\cdot g(dy\mid x)=f(B_{x}\mid x)\leq g(B_{x}\mid x)=\int_{B_{x}}1\cdot g(dy\mid x).

By definition of
B_{x}
, the converse inequality also holds, so
\int_{B_{x}}r(y,x)\cdot g(dy\mid x)=\int_{B_{x}}1\cdot g(dy\mid x)
. Let
q_{x}(y)=(r(y,x)-1)\cdot\chi(y\in B_{x})
. Then
q\geq 0
, and also
\int_{B_{x}}q_{x}(y)\cdot g(dy\mid x)=0
. Therefore,
q_{x}
is
g(-\mid x)

-almost-surely zero, and thus
r(-,x)\leq 1
, almost surely. We now set

\displaystyle p(y,x)=\begin{cases}r(y,x),&\text{if }r(y,x)\leq 1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

This
p
then satisfies
0\leq p\leq 1
, and
f(A\mid x)=\int_{A}p(y,x)\cdot g(dy\mid x)
for all
A\in\sigma_{Y}
.

Finally, we check that
p
is jointly measurable. This is easy, since for
any measurable
T\subseteq[0,1]
we have

\displaystyle p^{-1}(T)=\begin{cases}r^{-1}(T),&\text{if }0\notin T,\\
r^{1}(T)\cup r^{-1}((1,\infty)),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

From the previous proposition it is easy to see that
\mathsf{BorelStoch}_{\leq 1}

also satisfies the sharp witness property. The argument is very
similar to what we presented for
\mathsf{FinStoch}_{\leq 1}
.

Cartesian restriction categories

We now instantiate Definition
3.1
in
cartesian
restriction categories
. Such categories have a canonical poset
enrichment
[
CL02
, §2.1.4]
, where
f\leq g
if and only if

f\preceq g
. This means that
f
is a restriction of
g
on a smaller
domain. Since all morphisms are deterministic,
cartesian restriction
categories
satisfy the sharp witness property.

Proposition 3.19
.

In a
cartesian restriction category
, the conditional
preorder and the restriction order coincide:
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g
if and
only if
f\preceq g
.

Proof 3.20
.

Since
cartesian restriction categories
are
balanced
and satisfy the
sharp witness property, this is immediate from Proposition

3.15
.

Cartesian bicategories of relations

Let us instantiate Definition
3.1
in
cartesian
bicategories of relations
. These also have a canonical poset enrichment where

f\leq g
means that
f
is a ‘subrelation’ of
g
, in the following
sense:

(1)

This presentation of the poset enrichment is equivalent to the usual
one
[
Nes24
, Lemma 4.1.5]
. The next proposition relates the two
orderings.

Proposition 3.21
.

In a
cartesian bicategory of relations
, for two parallel
morphisms
f,g\colon X\to A
,
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g
if and only
if
f\leq g
.

Proof 3.22
.

(\Rightarrow)
We apply
Proposition
3.10

because
(\leq)
is also subunital.

(\Leftarrow)
If
f\leq g
(
i
), then we may take

r=(\mathrm{id}{}\otimes f)\mathbin{\fatsemi}\mu\mathbin{\fatsemi}\varepsilon
and
obtain that
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g
by the Frobenius axioms (
ii
).

Every morphism in a
cartesian bicategory of relations
is
quasi-total. However, since these categories are not

balanced
, the restriction order may differ from the conditional
preorder. The following example demonstrates that this is indeed the
case.

Example 3.23
.

Let
R,S\subseteq\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}
be morphisms in

\mathsf{Rel}
, given by
R=\{(1,2)\}
and
S=\{(1,2),(1,3)\}
.
Then
R\leq S
, but
R\not\preceq S
, since
\delta\mathbin{\fatsemi}(R\otimes(S\mathbin{\fatsemi}\varepsilon))=R\neq S
.

4
Least conditionals

Asking
partial Markov categories
to have unique conditionals is too
strong. In any
partial Markov category
with unique conditionals,
f\mathbin{\fatsemi}\varepsilon_{Y}=g\mathbin{\fatsemi}\varepsilon_{Y}
implies
f=g
for all parallel maps
f,g\colon X\to Y

[
DR23
]
. As a special case, Markov
categories with unique conditionals are posetal, see

[
Fri20
, Remark 11.16]
.

However, once we have an order in
partial Markov categories
, there
might be a canonical choice of conditional, namely the smallest among
all
conditionals. In this section, we consider least conditionals with
respect to two
orders on quasi-total maps: the conditional preorder

({\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq})
and the restriction order
(\preceq)
.

Definition 4.1
.

(Least conditionals)
Let
f:X\to Y\otimes Z
be a morphism in a (locally small)
partial Markov
category
. Write
C_{f}=\{c\colon Z\otimes X\to Y\mid f=(f\fatsemi(\mathrm{id}{}\otimes\varepsilon))\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}c\}
for the set of (quasi-total)

conditionals

of
f
. Now, we say that a

conditional
,
g\in C_{f}
, is

(1)

a
{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}
-least conditional of
f
when it is a least
element of

C_{f}
, ordered by the conditional preorder,
({\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq})
;

(2)

or, a
\preceq
-least conditional of
f
if it is the least
element of
C_{f}
ordered by the restriction order

(\preceq)
.

By Lemma
3.12
, every
(
\preceq
)-least
conditional
is a (
{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}
)-least

conditional
.

4.1
Least conditionals and copy-discard-compare categories

We demonstrate how least conditionals are related to the existence of
comparators. We start by characterizing
conditionals
of copy and
identity maps in a
copy-discard category
.

Lemma 4.2
.

Let
\mathsf{C}
be a
copy-discard category
.

(1)

A morphism
f\colon X\otimes X\to X
is a

conditional
of the copy
\delta_{X}\colon X\to X\otimes X
if and only if
\delta_{X}\fatsemi f=\mathrm{id}_{X}
.

(2)

A morphism
g\colon X\otimes X\to I

is a
conditional
of the identity
\mathrm{id}_{X}\colon X\to X
if and only
if
\delta_{X}\fatsemi g=\varepsilon_{X}
.

Note that the condition of Item (
1
) holds by
definition of the multiplication (
\mu_{X}
). Similarly, the definition
of the
cap

(\cap_{X})
contains the condition of
Item (
2
).

Proof 4.3
.

For point (i), suppose that
\delta_{X}\fatsemi f=\mathrm{id}_{X}
. Then, the defining equation
of conditionals can be derived as below left. Conversely, if
f
is a
conditional of
\delta_{X}
, then the middle equality on the right holds by
definition. Is then easy to see that
\delta_{X}\fatsemi f=\mathrm{id}_{X}
.

For point (ii), suppose that
\delta_{X}\mathbin{\fatsemi}g=\varepsilon_{X}
. Then, the
defining equation of conditionals can be derived as below left.
Conversely, discarding the output on both sides of the equality on the left
below shows
\delta_{X}\mathbin{\fatsemi}g=\varepsilon_{X}
, as below right.

Lemma 4.4
.

Let
\mathsf{C}
be a
copy-discard category
. If
f\colon X\otimes X\to X
is a

conditional
of the copy
\delta_{X}\colon X\to X\otimes X
, then
f\fatsemi\varepsilon_{X}\colon X\otimes X\to I

is a
conditional
of the identity map
\mathrm{id}_{X}\colon X\to X
. Moreover, if
f
is
the
\preceq
-least conditional of
\delta_{X}
then
f\fatsemi\varepsilon_{X}
is the

\preceq
-least conditional of
\mathrm{id}_{X}
.

Proof 4.5
.

By Lemma
4.2
,
f\fatsemi\varepsilon_{X}
is a conditional of the identity.
Now assume that
f
is the
\preceq
-least conditional of the copy map,
and let
g\colon X\otimes X\to I
be a conditional of the identity. We have to show that

f\fatsemi\varepsilon_{X}\preceq g
. Let
t=(\mathrm{id}_{X}\otimes\delta_{X})\fatsemi(g\otimes\mathrm{id}_{X})
. Step

(a)
below left uses that
g
is a
conditional
of the identity to show that
this
t
is a conditional of the copy map
\delta_{X}
. Since
f
is the

\preceq
-least conditional of the copy map,
\delta_{X}
, then
f\preceq t
(below right).

Discarding both sides of the above equation yields
f\fatsemi\varepsilon_{X}\preceq g
.

We are ready to show that, if they exist, comparators and
caps
are least
conditionals.

Theorem 4.6
.

Let
\mathsf{C}
be a
copy-discard-compare category
. The multiplication
\mu_{X}\colon X\otimes X\to X
is the
\preceq
-least conditional of the copy map
\delta_{X}\colon X\to X\otimes X
. The
cap
,
\cap_{X}\colon X\otimes X\to I
, is the least conditional of
the identity
\mathrm{id}_{X}\colon X\to X
with respect to the restriction
order
(\preceq)
. By Lemma

3.12
,

\mu_{X}
and
\cap_{X}
are also
{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}
-least conditionals.

Proof 4.7
.

By Lemma
4.2
,
\mu_{X}
and
\cap_{X}
are conditionals of the copy and identity maps, respectively.
We show that
\mu_{X}
is the
\preceq
-least conditional of
\delta_{X}
.
Let
f\colon X\otimes X\to X
be any conditional of the copy map.
Using
(i)
the Frobenius equations and
(ii)
Lemma
4.2
, we show that
f\preceq\mu_{X}
.

By Lemma
4.4
, the cap is the

\preceq
-least conditional of identity.

Since
\preceq
-least conditionals are unique, the following is an
immediate consequence of the previous proposition.

Corollary 4.8
.

A
copy-discard category
can admit at most one
copy-discard-compare

structure.

Next, we prove a converse to Theorem
4.6
. We
demonstrate that, under certain conditions, least conditionals of copier maps
give rise to a
copy-discard-compare structure
. As it turns out, one needs
to consider the restriction order
\preceq
to prove the
following
proposition.

Theorem 4.9
.

Let
\mathsf{C}
be a
copy-discard category
, and assume the following.

(1)

All copy maps
\delta_{X}\colon X\to X\otimes X
have a
\preceq
-least
conditional,
\mu_{X}\colon X\otimes X\to X
. By
Lemma
4.4
, the identity maps then also have

\preceq
-least conditionals
\cap_{X}=\mu_{X}\fatsemi\varepsilon_{X}\colon X\otimes X\to I
.

(2)

The family of conditionals
\cap_{X}
satisfy Item
(
4
) of
Definition
2.11
.

In this situation, the conditionals
\cap_{X}
satisfy the axioms of

caps
. By Proposition
2.12
,
\mathsf{C}
is thus a

copy-discard-compare category
.

Proof 4.10
.

We show that the equations
(
1
)-(
3
) of
Definition
2.11
are satisfied. The equality (
2
)

\delta_{X}\mathbin{\fatsemi}\cap_{X}=\varepsilon_{X}
holds by Lemma
4.2
. We
show commutativity. Using commutativity of the copy map and equality
(i)
,
we obtain that
\delta_{X}\fatsemi\sigma_{X,X}\fatsemi\cap_{X}=\varepsilon_{X}
also holds (below
left). By Lemma
4.2
, this implies that
\sigma_{X,X}\fatsemi\cap_{X}
is also a conditional of
\mathrm{id}_{X}
. Therefore,
\cap_{X}\preceq\sigma_{X,X}\fatsemi\cap_{X}
. We use this fact in steps
(a)
and
(c)
below right.
Step
(b)
applies naturality of the symmetries.

At last, we need to show equation (
3
), whose two sides
we name
t
and
u
.

Using coassociativity of copy, equality
(i)
and counitality of copy, one
can easily show that
\delta\fatsemi t=\mathrm{id}=\delta\fatsemi u
. By
Lemma
4.2
, we obtain that both
t
and
u
are

conditionals
of the copy
\delta_{X}\colon X\to X\otimes X
. We now prove that
t=\mu_{X}=u
. Steps marked with
(a)
use minimality of
\mu_{X}
.
Equations
(b)
use associativity and commutativity of the copier. Steps
(c)

use that
\cap_{X}
is quasi-total.

This shows that
\mathsf{C}
is a
copy-discard category
with
caps
,
which, by Proposition
2.12
, is also a

copy-discard-compare
category.

The following is an immediate consequence of the previous theorem and
Proposition
3.15
.

Corollary 4.11
.

Let
\mathsf{C}
be a
balanced

partial Markov category

that satisfies the
sharp witness property. Assume
that the copier and identity maps have
{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}
-least
conditionals

\mu_{X}
and
\cap_{X}
, and that the
\cap_{X}
maps satisfy
Item (
4
) of
Definition
2.11
. Then
\mathsf{C}
is a
discrete
partial Markov category
.

4.2
Examples

Proposition 4.12
.

The category
\mathsf{FinStoch}_{\leq 1}
is
balanced
and satisfies the
sharp witness property. Therefore,
\preceq
-least
conditionals
are the same as
{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}
-least conditionals.

Given
f\colon X\to A\otimes B
, write
\|f(-\mid x)\|=\sum_{b^{\prime}\in B}f(a,b^{\prime}\mid x)
for the total mass of the
subdistribution
f(-\mid x)
. The least
conditional
c_{0}:A\otimes X\to B
of
f

is given by

\displaystyle c_{0}(b\mid a,x)

\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\frac{f(a,b\mid x)}{\sum_{b^{\prime}\in B}f(a,b^{\prime}\mid x)}&\text{if
}\|f(-\mid x)\|\neq 0,\\
0&\text{if
}\|f(-\mid x)\|=0.\end{cases}

Let
x\in X
such that
\|f(-\mid x)\|\neq 0
. Then, for any

conditional
,
c:A\otimes X\to B
, of
f
, the value
c(b\mid a,x)
is forced
to be equal to
c_{0}(b\mid a,x)
. If
\|f(-\mid x)\|=0
, then
c(-\mid a,x)
could be any subdistribution. The least conditional is the solution that
contains no ‘junk information’.

The category
\mathsf{BorelStoch}_{\leq 1}
does not have all least
conditionals
.
We demonstrate this via the following example, adapted from

[
Cho19
, Remark 5.2.10]
.

Example 4.13
.

Let
\mu
be the Lebesgue-measure on the unit interval
[0,1]
,
viewed as a morphism
\mu:1\to[0,1]\otimes 1
in

\mathsf{BorelStoch}_{\leq 1}
. Quasi-total
conditionals

c:[0,1]\otimes 1\to 1
of
\mu
correspond to Lebesgue-measurable
subsets
C\subseteq[0,1]
such that for all measurable
B\subseteq[0,1]
,
\mu(B)=\mu(B\cap C)
. The restriction
order
(\preceq)
and the pointwise order
({\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq})

coincide on these conditionals, and translate to subset inclusion
on measurable subsets.

For an
\alpha\in[0,1]
, the set
C_{\alpha}=[0,1]\setminus\{\alpha\}
satisfies
\mu(B)=\mu(B\cap C_{\alpha})
for
all
measurable
B
. Therefore, a least conditional
C_{0}
must satisfy

C_{0}\subseteq B_{\alpha}
for all
\alpha\in[0,1]
. But such a

C_{0}
can only be the empty set
\emptyset
, which does not
satisfy
\mu(B\cap\emptyset)=\mu(B)
for all measurable
B
.
Therefore, a least conditional of
\mu
cannot exist.

By Proposition
3.19
,

\preceq
-least conditionals are the same as
{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}
-least
conditionals in a discrete cartesian restriction category.

Proposition 4.14
.

Any discrete cartesian restriction category has least conditionals. Given a
map
f:X\to A\otimes B
, the least conditional of
f
is given by
c_{0}=(\mathrm{id}{}\otimes f)\fatsemi((\mu\fatsemi\varepsilon)\otimes\mathrm{id}{})
.

Proof 4.15
.

We check that this is indeed a quasi-total
conditional
. It
is quasi-total because every morphism is deterministic
(
i
). We check
the
conditional
equation using the partial Frobenius axioms
(
ii
).

Then,
c_{0}\leq c
.

To provide intuition, we explicitly describe least conditionals in

\mathsf{Par}
. The situation is very similar to
\mathsf{FinStoch}_{\leq 1}
. Let
f:X\rightharpoonup A\otimes B
be a partial function. Let
x\in X
such that

f(x)
is defined and equal to
(a,b)
. Every conditional
c:A\times X\rightharpoonup B
has to satisfy
c(a,x)=b
. If
a\neq a^{\prime}
, then

c(a^{\prime},x)
can be anything. Similarly, if
f(x)
is undefined,

c(a^{\prime},x)
can be arbitrary. The least conditional
c_{0}
is undefined
in all such cases. Formally,

\displaystyle c_{0}(a,x)=\begin{cases}b&\text{ if }f(x)\text{ is defined and }f(x)=(a,b)\\
\text{undefined}&\text{ otherwise}\end{cases}.

Proposition 4.16
.

Any
cartesian bicategory of relations
has
\preceq
-least

conditionals
.

Proof 4.17
.

By Proposition
2.16
, the morphism
c_{0}=(\mathrm{id}{}\otimes f)\fatsemi((\mu\fatsemi\varepsilon)\otimes\mathrm{id}{})
is a quasi-total
conditional
of

f\colon X\to A\otimes B
. Suppose there is another quasi-total

conditional
,
c\colon A\otimes X\to B
, of
f
.

We use that (
i
)
c
is a conditional of
f
, and (
ii
) the
Frobenius axioms of
cartesian bicategories of relations
to show that
c_{0}\preceq c
.

5
Updates increase validity

In its most general form, bayesian updating involves a prior
distribution and a (fuzzy) evidence predicate. From these inputs, one
can compute a posterior distribution by incorporating the evidence
into the prior.

Given a distribution
\sigma
and a predicate
p
, the validity of
p
in
\sigma
is a
real number in the unit interval
[0,1]
. This validity expresses the
probability that the predicate
p
holds for a random sample from
\sigma
.

A key property of bayesian updating is that the validity of the
evidence is
greater or equal in the posterior than in the prior. A proof of this fact for
discrete probability can be found in
[
Jac19
, Theorem 2.1]
.
Ultimately, the result is a consequence of the well-known Cauchy–Schwarz
inequality. The
Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
states that the square of the
inner product of two vectors
u,v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
is smaller than the product of
their squared norms:

\left(\sum\nolimits_{i}u_{i}\cdot v_{i}\right)^{2}\leq\left(\sum\nolimits_{i}u_{i}^{2}\right)\cdot\left(\sum\nolimits_{j}v_{j}^{2}\right).

The inequality also holds if we allow parameters
x
,
y
and

z
, thus considering families of vectors
h:X\to\mathbb{R}^{n}

f:Y\to\mathbb{R}^{n}
, and
g:Z\to\mathbb{R}^{n}
. If we write
f_{i}(x)
for

f(x)_{i}
(similarly for
g
and
h
) and let
u_{i}=\sqrt{h_{i}(x)}\cdot f_{i}(y)
and
v_{j}=\sqrt{h_{j}(x)}\cdot g_{j}(z)
, the
Cauchy–Schwarz inequality becomes:

\immediate\immediate\left(\sum\nolimits_{i}h_{i}(x)\cdot f_{i}(y)\cdot g_{i}(z)\right)^{2}\leq\left(\sum\nolimits_{i}h_{i}(x)\cdot f_{i}(y)^{2}\right)\cdot\left(\sum\nolimits_{j}h_{j}(x)\cdot g_{j}(z)^{2}\right).

(2)

We consider this general form and express it synthetically, using the
conditional preorder.

Definition 5.1
.

(Cauchy–Schwarz inequality)
A
discrete partial Markov category
satisfies the

Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
if, for all triples of morphisms
h\colon X\to A
,
f\colon A\to Y
, and
g\colon A\to Z
, the following inequality holds.

Example 5.2
.

Instantiating the above definition in
\mathsf{FinStoch}_{\leq 1}
yields precisely the
usual
Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
(
2
). Therefore,

\mathsf{FinStoch}_{\leq 1}
satisfies the synthetic
Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
.

Example 5.3
.

The
Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
holds as equality in
discrete
cartesian restriction categories
.

Example 5.4
.

cartesian bicategories of relations
satisfy the

Cauchy–Schwarz
inequality
.

Proposition 5.5
.

A
partial Markov category
that satisfies the
Cauchy–Schwarz
inequality
also satisfies the inequality below, called the
means
inequality
, for all
u\colon X\to A
and
v\colon A\to Y
.

Remark 5.7
.

(QM-AM inequality)

The means inequality owes its name to the inequality between the
weighted arithmetic and quadratic means of a vector of positive
real numbers,
x{}_{1},\dots,x_{n}

with weights
w{}_{1}+\dots+w_{n}=1
.

\left(\sum\nolimits_{i\in I}w_{i}\cdot x_{i}\right)^{2}\leq\sum\nolimits_{i\in I}w_{i}\cdot x_{i}^{2}.

Example 5.8
.

The
partial Markov category
of substochastic channels,

\mathsf{FinStoch}_{\leq 1}
, satisfies the
means inequality
.
In particular, if
f
is a state
\sigma:I\to X
, and
g
is a predicate
p:X\to I
, then the means inequality gives the well-known inequality between expectations of random variables, usually written as
E[X]^{2}\leq E[X^{2}]
.

With this setup, we can work towards a synthetic analogue of
the validity-increase theorem. We start by providing the relevant
definitions.

Definition 5.9
.

(Validity)

In a
partial Markov category
, the
validity
of a predicate
p\colon X\to I

with respect to a prior
\sigma\colon I\to X
is the scalar
obtained by composition,

(\sigma\fatsemi p)
.

We first prove a special case of the validity increase theorem for deterministic evidence.

Proposition 5.10
.

In a
partial Markov category
, updating a prior state
\sigma:I\to X
with a
deterministic predicate,
p:X\to I
, increases the predicate’s posterior
validity. That is,

\sigma\fatsemi p{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}p^{\dagger}_{\sigma}\fatsemi p.

Proof 5.11
.

The
conditional
equation for the
bayesian inverse
is
\sigma\fatsemi\delta_{X}\fatsemi(p\otimes\mathrm{id}_{X})=(\sigma\fatsemi p)\otimes p^{\dagger}_{\sigma}
. Therefore,
\sigma\fatsemi\delta_{X}\fatsemi(p\otimes\mathrm{id}_{X}){\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}p^{\dagger}_{\sigma}
; and, as a consequence,
\sigma\fatsemi p=\sigma\fatsemi\delta_{X}\fatsemi(p\otimes p){\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}p^{\dagger}_{\sigma}\fatsemi p
.

When the predicate
p
is not necessarily deterministic, we will
need the
means inequality
and the following notion of zero
scalars.

Definition 5.12
.

Let
\mathsf{C}
be a
copy-discard category
.

(1)

A scalar
s:I\to I
is called a zero scalar, if it
satisfies
s\otimes f=s\otimes g
for all
f,g:X\to Y
. Any scalar that does
not satisfy this property is said to be non-zero.

(2)

We say that the non-zero scalars in
\mathsf{C}
are
cancellative if
s\otimes f=s\otimes g
implies
f=g
for all
f,g:X\to Y
and non-zero scalar
s:I\to I
.

Example 5.13
.

Non-zero scalars in
\mathsf{BorelStoch}_{\leq 1}
are
cancellative. Scalars correspond to
elements of the unit interval
[0,1]
. Given a subprobability
kernel
f:(X,\sigma_{X})\to(Y,\sigma_{Y})
,
the tensor product
s\otimes f
is given by
pointwise multiplication with
s\in[0,1]
. That is for
x\in X
and
A\in\sigma_{Y}
,

(s\otimes f)(A\mid x)=s\cdot f(A\mid x).

Clearly, if
s\neq 0
, then
s\otimes f=s\otimes g
implies

f=g
for parallel subprobability kernels
f
and
g
.
Similarly, non-zero scalars in
\mathsf{FinStoch}_{\leq 1}
are also
cancellative.

Lemma 5.14
.

Let
\mathsf{C}
be a
copy-discard category
whose non-zero scalars are
cancellative. Then, the following cancellation property holds for the

conditional inequality
. If
s:I\to I
is a non-zero scalar and
f,g:X\to Y
, then
s\otimes f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}s\otimes g
implies
f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}g
.

Proof 5.15
.

Let
s\otimes f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}_{r}s\otimes g
. Then, by definition
f\otimes s=(s\otimes g)\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}r=s\otimes(g\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}r)
. By cancellativity,
f=g\hyperlink{linkTriangleComposition}{\mathbin{\triangleleft}}r
, and thus

f{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}_{r}g
.

Theorem 5.16
.

Let
\mathsf{C}
be a
partial Markov category
that satisfies the

means inequality
and whose non-zero scalars are cancellative.
Then, updating a prior state with a predicate increases the
predicate’s validity in the posterior. That is, for all
\sigma:I\to X
and
p:X\to I
,

\sigma\fatsemi p{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}p^{\dagger}_{\sigma}\fatsemi p.

Proof 5.17
.

We apply the
means inequality
in the following calculation.

Since the non-zero scalars are cancellative, we conclude that
\sigma\fatsemi p{\color[rgb]{0.2969,0.3359,0.4141}\sqsubseteq}p^{\hyperlink{linkbayesinv}{\dagger}}_{\sigma}\fatsemi p
, because the scalar is either zero or cancellative.

Notably,
\mathsf{FinStoch}_{\leq 1}
satisfies the assumptions of the previous
theorem. Therefore, we have synthetically recovered

[
Jac19
, Theorem 2.1]
. Also observe that the proof
of Theorem
5.16
does not rely on the
full power of the means inequality. The instance we used in the
proof of Theorem
5.16
holds in

\mathsf{BorelStoch}_{\leq 1}
, as the
following example demonstrates.

Example 5.18
.

Let
(X,\sigma_{X})
be standard Borel, and
\mu
a subprobability
measure on
X
. The collection of
\mu
-integrable functions
X\to\mathbb{R}
, quotiented by
\mu
-almost-sure equality, forms a real
inner product space with inner product
\langle p,q\rangle=\int p(x)\cdot q(x)\cdot\mu(dx)
. Therefore, one
can apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to get

\Bigl(\int p(x)\cdot\mu(dx)\Bigr)^{2}=\langle p,\varepsilon_{X}\rangle^{2}\leq\langle p,p\rangle\cdot\langle\varepsilon_{X},\varepsilon_{X}\rangle=\Bigl(\int p(x)^{2}\cdot\mu(dx)\Bigr)\cdot\Bigl(\int 1\cdot\mu(dx)\Bigr)\leq\int p(x)^{2}\cdot\mu(dx).

6
Concluding remarks

We introduced a novel preorder enrichment in the general setting of

partial Markov categories
; we showed that it generalizes the canonical preorder
enrichments of two categories of probability kernels,
cartesian restriction
categories
, and
cartesian bicategories of relations
. We showed how
comparators relate to least conditionals of copier maps. We axiomatized the

Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
and the quadratic-arithmetic
means
inequality
. From these, we abstractly derived the fact that Bayesian updating
increases the validity of the evidence in the posterior.

Further exploration of the basic theory of the
conditional inequality
is
warranted. One interesting question is about antisymmetry of the order, which is
related to inverses of scalars. An inverse of
s:I\to I
is a scalar
s^{-1}:I\to I
such that
s\otimes s^{-1}=\varepsilon_{I}
. Clearly,
conditional inequality
is
antisymmetric only if the only scalar with an inverse is

\varepsilon_{I}
. It is an open question whether the converse statement
holds. It would also be
interesting to find necessary conditions for the conditional preorder to form
an enrichment. Relatedly, the synthetic formulation of the
Cauchy–Schwarz
inequality
and the means inequality opens the way for a more refined
axiomatization: can we derive both from some more fundamental principle?

Finally, a potential application of the synthetic
means inequality
lies in
mixing it with the additive structure of some
partial Markov categories
,
like effectuses with copiers
[
CJWW15
]
. In that setting, it may be possible
to develop a synthetic theory of variance and covariance.

Figure 6
:
Structure and axioms of cartesian bicategories of relations.

Remark A.1
.

In every cartesian bicategory of relations, the copy and discard morphisms are not natural, but they are
lax natural
:
f\mathbin{\fatsemi}\delta\leq\delta\mathbin{\fatsemi}(f\otimes f)
and
f\mathbin{\fatsemi}\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon
(
Figure

7
, left).
Moreover, the comonoid structure is left adjoint to the monoid structure:
\mathrm{id}\leq\delta\mathbin{\fatsemi}\mu
,
\mu\mathbin{\fatsemi}\delta\leq\mathrm{id}
,
\mathrm{id}\leq\varepsilon\mathbin{\fatsemi}\eta
and
\eta\mathbin{\fatsemi}\varepsilon\leq\mathrm{id}
(
Figure

7
, middle and right).
In fact, the original definition of cartesian bicategory of relations assumed a poset enrichment satisfying these conditions
[
CW87
, Definitions 1.2 and 2.1]
.
The definition we give here (
Figure

6
) is equivalent to the original one
[
Nes24
, Lemma 4.1.6]
.

Figure 7
:
Comonoids in cartesian bicategories of relations are lax natural, and they are left adjoint to the monoids.

Lemma A.2
.

In a cartesian bicategory of relations, every morphism is
quasi-total.
